Adds a draft RFC defining canonical readiness conditions, plugin readiness providers, four standard hosting profiles, operator profile composition, CLI projections, compatibility behavior, and release-conformance expectations.

Reproducibility: yes. for the documentation defect: compare the RFC's pending-execution statement with the linked implementation PR's successful exact-head AWS Crabbox result. The proposed product behavior itself is not a current-main bug requiring reproduction.

target.title: RFC: Readiness Conditions and Standard Hosting Profiles
target.body:
## Decision requested

Should OpenClaw add canonical readiness conditions and standard hosting profiles?

The proposal normalizes existing Gateway signals into canonical readiness conditions, lets plugins publish additional conditions through readiness providers, and lets standard profiles compose those conditions. It extends Gateway `/ready` and `/readyz`, health, status, plugin activation, and `openclaw.json`. It does not add a policy engine, OCC dependency, or downstream hosting abstraction.

## Problem

OpenClaw can run in containers today, but process health does not prove that the selected runtime shape is usable.

Examples:

- A container starts while its Gateway remains loopback-only.
- A full workspace volume leaves HTTP alive while writes fail.
- A node controller starts before an approved controllable target is connected.
- Plugin diagnostics can be useful without making the entire Gateway unavailable.

Hosts currently close these gaps with private startup scripts and downstream-only checks. This RFC turns those checks into reusable runtime conditions and standard release-tested profiles.

## Modernizing existing readiness

Today `/ready` and `/readyz` are backed by a purpose-built Gateway evaluator over a fixed set of signals. Plugins cannot register callbacks, operators cannot enumerate or compose criteria, and the existing observations do not share a structured condition model.

This RFC commits to normalizing those existing observations, not leaving them as a permanent parallel system:

| Existing observation | Canonical condition | Requirement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Startup dependencies or sidecars are pending | `GatewayStartupComplete` | Required |
| Gateway is draining and rejects new work | `GatewayAcceptingWork` | Required |
| A selected channel has an unsuppressed runtime-health failure | `ChannelRuntimeReady` | Required |
| A selected channel is intentionally suppressed | `ChannelRuntimeSuppressed` | Advisory |
| Event-loop health is degraded or unavailable | `EventLoopHealthy` | Advisory initially, preserving current behavior |

```text
existing Gateway conditions
+ standard-profile conditions
+ plugin-provider conditions
-> one canonical /ready and /readyz result
```

Startup-pending details are retained in `GatewayStartupComplete`. Health and offline status surfaces without authoritative live observations report required core conditions as `Unknown` with stable `*NotChecked` reasons rather than omitting them or synthesizing success.

The legacy `failing`, `suppressed`, and `eventLoop` fields remain compatibility projections during migration. New consumers use `conditions`, `failures`, and `advisories`. Profiles and plugins cannot weaken or bypass the core Gateway conditions.
## Readiness providers

A readiness provider is a lifecycle-owned callback that publishes one observed condition.

Only an activated OpenClaw plugin can register executable provider code through `OpenClawPluginApi`. Core criteria use internal evaluators. Operators, host configuration, and OCC select profiles and reference provider IDs; they do not inject callbacks.

```ts
type PluginReadinessResult = {
  status: "True" | "False" | "Unknown";
  reason: string;
  message: string;
};

type PluginReadinessProvider = {
  id: string;
  description: string;
  check(context: {
    config: OpenClawConfig;
    pluginConfig: unknown;
    signal: AbortSignal;
  }): Promise<PluginReadinessResult> | PluginReadinessResult;
};

type RegisterReadinessCriterion = (
  provider: PluginReadinessProvider,
) => void;
```

Example:

```ts
api.registerReadinessCriterion({
  id: "backend",
  description: "Reports whether the plugin backend can accept work.",
  async check({ pluginConfig, signal }) {
    return (await probeBackend(pluginConfig, { signal }))
      ? { status: "True", reason: "BackendReady", message: "Backend is reachable." }
      : { status: "False", reason: "BackendUnavailable", message: "Backend is unreachable." };
  },
});
```

Core publishes this as `plugin.<plugin-id>.backend`. The Gateway invokes `check` asynchronously and owns namespacing, enumeration, validation, timeout, cancellation, caching, coalescing, and error conversion.

Provider checks must be read-only, idempotent, safe under repeated or concurrent invocation, cancellation-aware, and free of blocking synchronous I/O. Every active plugin provider is advisory by default. Only operator configuration can promote a provider to required.

## Standard profiles

OpenClaw ships a small catalog of standard profiles and validates them in release gates.

| Profile | Runtime posture | Additional readiness signals |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `local` | Default foreground or local runtime | Config, workspace, and Gateway evidence; plugin diagnostics are advisory. |
| `container` | Gateway directly reachable through a container listener | Effective listener is resolved and non-loopback. |
| `reverse-proxy` | Gateway behind a trusted identity proxy | Trusted-proxy auth has a user header and trusted source. |
| `node-mode` | Gateway controlling one or more execution targets | Pairing, connected target, command approval, and control-channel evidence. |

A profile describes runtime posture, not packaging. Docker behind an identity proxy selects `reverse-proxy`; directly reachable Docker selects `container`.

Selection is optional. Precedence is:

```text
gateway flag > environment > openclaw.json > local default
```

Profiles validate effective runtime state. They do not generate or repair configuration.

## Custom profiles and support

In v1, an operator profile extends one standard profile and may add required or advisory provider IDs. It cannot remove or weaken inherited conditions.

```json5
{
  hosting: {
    profile: "acme/managed",
    profiles: {
      "acme/managed": {
        extends: "container",
        requiredCriteria: ["plugin.storage.backend"],
        advisoryCriteria: ["plugin.metrics.exporter"],
      },
    },
  },
}
```

OpenClaw supports and release-tests the inherited standard profile. The plugin or operator owns added provider semantics and the extension's additional support promise.

A later revision may allow an operator to compose a profile without extending a standard profile. It would remain operator-owned and would still be conjoined with universal Gateway startup, drain, channel, and event-loop readiness.

## What the host sees

The selected profile and provider conditions are added to the existing Gateway ready result. They do not create a separate endpoint.

For example, a container starts with `hosting.profile: "container"`, but its effective Gateway listener is still loopback-only:

```console
$ curl -i http://127.0.0.1:18789/readyz
HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
```

The response bodies below are abridged to the fields and conditions relevant to each transition. The normative response also retains existing Gateway fields such as `failing` and `uptimeMs` and may contain other profile conditions.

```json
{
  "profile": "container",
  "ready": false,
  "conditions": [
    {
      "type": "GatewayResponding",
      "status": "True",
      "requirement": "required",
      "reason": "GatewayResponding",
      "message": "Gateway is responding."
    },
    {
      "type": "ContainerStateReady",
      "status": "False",
      "requirement": "required",
      "reason": "ContainerGatewayLoopback",
      "message": "The effective Gateway listener is loopback-only."
    }
  ],
  "failures": ["ContainerGatewayLoopback"],
  "advisories": []
}
```

After the effective listener becomes reachable, the same endpoint returns `200`. The host does not switch APIs or interpret a second readiness model:

```console
$ curl -i http://127.0.0.1:18789/readyz
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
```

```json
{
  "profile": "container",
  "ready": true,
  "conditions": [
    {
      "type": "GatewayResponding",
      "status": "True",
      "requirement": "required",
      "reason": "GatewayResponding",
      "message": "Gateway is responding."
    },
    {
      "type": "ContainerStateReady",
      "status": "True",
      "requirement": "required",
      "reason": "ContainerStateReady",
      "message": "The effective Gateway listener is reachable."
    }
  ],
  "failures": [],
  "advisories": []
}
```

A plugin provider is visible through the same result. Because plugin providers are advisory by default, a failed provider remains observable while HTTP readiness stays `200`:

```json
{
  "profile": "container",
  "ready": true,
  "conditions": [
    {
      "type": "plugin.storage.backend",
      "status": "False",
      "requirement": "advisory",
      "reason": "BackendUnavailable",
      "message": "Backend is unreachable."
    }
  ],
  "failures": [],
  "advisories": ["BackendUnavailable"]
}
```

If an operator profile promotes `plugin.storage.backend` to required, that same failed observation contributes to `failures` and changes `/readyz` to `503`. When the provider later reports `True`, `/readyz` returns to `200` without restarting OpenClaw.
## Canonical result

Every condition has:

```text
type + status + requirement + reason + message
```

| Requirement | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `required` | `False` or `Unknown` blocks readiness and appears in `failures`. |
| `advisory` | `False` or `Unknown` appears in `advisories` without changing HTTP 200 to 503. |

The same result appears through `/ready`, `/readyz`, health, and status. Existing Gateway lifecycle observations are normalized into required or advisory core conditions and remain authoritative. Unauthenticated remote probes retain their redacted boolean response.

## Existing demand

The RFC maps the proposal to reported readiness gaps including [#96084](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/96084), [#78136](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/78136), [#73652](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/73652), [#78954](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/78954), and [#43886](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/43886).

## Consolidated implementation

The complete initial implementation is available as [openclaw/openclaw#104018](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/104018). The fork PRs below remain review slices.

## Draft implementation stack

| Slice | Draft PR |
| --- | --- |
| Canonical core conditions and local profile | [PR 17](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/17) (`cc9c4246`) |
| Standard profile selection and predicates | [PR 18](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/18) (`39a3b947`) |
| Node-mode readiness | [PR 19](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/19) (`270f7a3d`) |
| Workspace writability | [PR 22](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/22) (`5723f664`) |
| Readiness providers and operator profiles | [PR 23](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/23) (`399cf745`) |
| Canonical readiness CLI | [PR 27](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/27) (`fe4c51c1`) |

The final composed stack passes 196 focused assertions across readiness, Gateway, status JSON, package acceptance, and Docker planning.

The optional final CLI slice adds `openclaw ready` as a thin projection of the live Gateway result. Human output lists structured conditions, `--json` preserves the canonical successful result, and its exit status fails closed for required failures, unknowns, transport errors, or a missing readiness contract while advisory findings remain successful.

Making that lane a blocking release gate is intentionally deferred until contract acceptance and successful packaged Docker proof. [Fork PR 21](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/21) demonstrates the separate workflow change without coupling this implementation to a permanent release obligation.

The stack includes a package-installed Docker conformance lane. Its deterministic plan and release wiring are implemented; execution of the newest workspace-volume scenario remains pending because Docker was unavailable on the authoring host.

## Bounded evaluation

Readiness calls have layered code-owned budgets: one second per plugin provider, one second for workspace probing, one second for the complete node-pairing condition, and an independent two-second outer watchdog. A stalled pairing store yields required `Unknown` with stable reason `NodePairingTimedOut`. Workspace, provider, and node evaluation run concurrently.

A provider timeout becomes `Unknown` without depending on callback cancellation. Required timeouts yield `503`; advisory timeouts remain visible without blocking. If the complete evaluation exceeds its outer budget, `/ready` and `/readyz` fail closed with `503` rather than hanging or reporting ready.

Core evaluators use bounded snapshot work. In-process timers cannot interrupt synchronous JavaScript that blocks the Node event loop, so provider callbacks must be observational and non-blocking; worker/process isolation for malicious plugins is outside this RFC.
## Completion roadmap

The initial stack establishes the contract; completing the support promise remains explicit work:

1. Finish the canonical core and activation conditions:
   - Strengthen ConfigLoaded so it proves the validated effective runtime snapshot is installed, not merely that a source file parsed.
   - Add conditional required RequiredPluginsActivated while keeping general PluginsLoaded advisory.
   - Add required RequiredSecretsAvailable from the redacted startup secrets snapshot.
   - Add required ModelRoutingResolved for profiles that accept agent work, using resolved startup state without issuing a model request.
   - Keep ProfileSelected as proof that hosting-profile precedence was applied.
   - Continue projecting startup, drain, channel, event-loop, workspace, topology, and node observations through the same condition model.

   These checks are bounded reads over startup snapshots. Readiness polling does not reload plugins, resolve secrets, contact a model, or mutate configuration. Brokered egress belongs in a derived profile/provider, no-runtime-secrets posture belongs in conformance, and checkpoint freshness/safe destruction belong in Runtime Continuity.
2. Keep /ready, /readyz, health, status, and openclaw ready as projections of one result while /healthz remains shallow liveness.
3. Preserve bounded provider execution with enumeration, deadlines, cancellation, cache/coalescing, and a fail-closed outer watchdog.
4. Execute the package-installed Docker matrix on Linux, including deterministic failure and recovery scenarios, and publish immutable evidence tied to the OpenClaw artifact/version, selected profile, and condition-contract version. Project that evidence through the same readiness result:
   - ArtifactIdentityAvailable reports the running packaged artifact identity and is advisory for source/development runs.
   - SelectedProfileConformant reports whether matching packaged release evidence passed for the selected profile; operator profiles may require it.
   - ExpectedArtifactMatched is required when a host supplies an immutable expected artifact identity.

   Readiness reads packaged metadata; it does not rerun conformance tests. This is release evidence for hosting profiles, not a general compatibility, upgrade, or migration system.
5. After contract acceptance and successful proof, promote the standard-profile matrix into blocking package-acceptance release conformance.
6. Define stable, redacted readiness-transition events; hosts remain responsible for telemetry sinks, dashboards, and alerts.
7. Add later Doctor/lint findings and safe recommendations without making Doctor, policy, or plugins dependencies of core readiness.

Readiness and continuity stay distinct: /ready says whether this runtime can serve work. Dirty/synced state, checkpoint publication, and a generation-fenced safe-to-destroy result belong to the separate Runtime Continuity contract. A runtime may be ready but dirty, or not ready but synced.
## Boundaries

- Existing installations default to `local`.
- Standard profiles work without optional plugins.
- Doctor and policy may consume readiness later but are not dependencies.
- Docker, Kubernetes, and systemd own probe timing and retries.
- OCC may select a profile, but readiness remains in the runtime plane.
- AgentHarness traffic and events do not enter this contract.







## Packaged evidence and Lobster removal

Release conformance now has a minimal artifact-bound record: artifact version/package identity/digest, selected profile, condition-contract version, required condition types, result, suite identity, completion time, and optional build provenance. Readiness validates immutable packaged metadata; it never reruns release tests.

This feeds ArtifactIdentityAvailable, SelectedProfileConformant, and ExpectedArtifactMatched through the existing canonical result. It is not a general upgrade or migration framework.

The Lobster exit gate is explicit: once a packaged OpenClaw release passes the selected profile and activation-condition matrix, Lobster removes matching private startup probes, patch-presence checks, and exact startup-checklist tests.





## ClawBus readiness

A selected standard or operator profile may require canonical ClawBus families or host-provider versions. RequiredClawBusCapabilitiesAvailable reads the live generation-bound negotiated session snapshot and fails closed for a missing session, generation mismatch, missing capability, or unavailable status. Readiness does not probe remote host services on every call.

Reproducibility: not applicable. This PR proposes a new architecture and CLI contract rather than reporting broken existing behavior.
